research.title: Research Overview
paragraphs: A researcher working between first-person experience and third-person measurement, asking what each can reveal that the other cannot.
Hi, I'm Cyra! 👋 I really love beautiful things — from beauty itself to research that's beautiful in how it's made.
Lately I'm into interoception, consciousness, and affective science across methods, with side quests into language models and AI. I come at it from computational methods.
Off the clock: yoga, books and writing, fashion, and video games.

recent.body: Started as a real-time Korean–English medical interpreter at The Peak Clinic (dermatology), Seoul — for part-time cash, and to help out a friend.
Joined the Embodied Computation Group (Aarhus University & Cambridge Psychiatry) as a remote research intern — LLMs, interoception, and consciousness.
Rejoined UPenn Department of Psychiatry as remote research intern — multimodal AI scoring of therapist interpersonal skills.
Presented an AYUI immunology poster on Treg biology, mechanisms, and therapeutic potential at the STEM Union Academic Conference 2026.
ARR reviews received — withdrawing short paper this cycle to resubmit as long paper for the next.
Joined Shanghai AI Laboratory as RA for AI4BioSci / SciForge — contributing to verification-oriented scientific-agent infrastructure.
Joined the Clinical Neuroscience of Anxiety and Depression (CAD) Lab at Yonsei University (Dr. Juyeon Hur / 허주연) as RA — studying interoception and vulnerability mechanisms in anxiety and depression.

earlier.body: Presented "Predicting Next-Day Suicidal Urges, Depression, and PTSD Symptoms Using EMA and Passive Sensing" at the Association for Behavioral and Cognitive Therapies Annual Convention.
Joined UPenn Department of Psychiatry as RA — working on a research project.
Joined Stanford Psychophysiology Lab as RA — developing reproducible R pipelines for 10,000+ EMA and sleep diary records.
Took leave of absence — returned home to recover, cared for grandpa and cat Guagua 🐱
JASP paper published — "Underestimating Others' Positive Attitude Toward AI Reduces Intentions to Adopt AI in Various Business Contexts" in the Journal of Applied Social Psychology (56(6), 443-456).
Exchange at Washington University in St. Louis — joined Speech & Hearing Lab; started clinical shadowing at CID and IDDRC.
BJSP paper published — "Perceived Economic Inequality Inhibits Pro-Environmental Engagement" in the British Journal of Social Psychology (64(2), e12815).
Presented "Neural Fatigue From Speech Perception in Noise and Social Withdrawal" at the Chinese University of Hong Kong Brain and Mind Institute.

ai-attitude-underestimation.title: Underestimating others' positive attitude toward AI reduces intentions to adopt AI in various business contexts
ai-attitude-underestimation.authors: Rongmian Huo, Shasha Yang, Cai Dong, Sijing Chen
ai-attitude-underestimation.summary: Across three preregistered studies (N = 826), we find that people systematically underestimate how positively others view AI adoption. This underestimation gap reduces personal AI adoption intentions, mediated by decreased perceived social norms for AI use.
ai-attitude-underestimation.motivation: AI adoption in business contexts depends not only on personal attitudes but also on perceived social norms—what we believe others think about AI. Prior research documented an "AI attitude asymmetry" where individuals hold more positive attitudes than they attribute to others. However, the consequences of this perception gap for actual adoption intentions remained unexplored. This study bridges social psychology and technology adoption research by examining how pluralistic ignorance about AI attitudes shapes individual decision-making across diverse business domains.
ai-attitude-underestimation.methodology: Three preregistered online studies (total N = 826) using between-subjects and within-subjects designs with representative US samples via Prolific. Participants rated their own AI adoption attitudes and estimated others' attitudes across hiring, healthcare, education, and customer service contexts. We measured perceived social norms, personal AI adoption intentions, and manipulated the target of comparison (general others vs. specific peers). Mediation analyses tested the indirect path from underestimation gap → perceived norms → adoption intentions. All materials, data, and analysis code are openly available.
ai-attitude-underestimation.results: Participants consistently underestimated others' AI-positive attitudes across all business contexts (d = 0.48–0.71). The underestimation gap negatively predicted personal AI adoption intentions (β = −0.31, p < .001), mediated by perceived social norms (indirect effect = −0.14, 95% CI [−0.21, −0.08]). The effect held across demographic groups and was robust to comparison target manipulation. Correcting the misperception in an exploratory condition increased adoption intentions, suggesting a causal pathway.
ai-attitude-underestimation.impact: This work provides the first systematic evidence that pluralistic ignorance about AI attitudes is a barrier to technology adoption. It extends the "AI attitude asymmetry" literature by demonstrating behavioral consequences beyond attitude measurement, and offers practical implications: correcting misperceptions about peer attitudes could be a lightweight intervention to increase AI adoption in organizational settings. The open-science workflow (preregistration, open materials, data, code) serves as a template for reproducible social psychology research.

inequality-proenvironment.title: Perceived Economic Inequality Inhibits Pro-Environmental Engagement
inequality-proenvironment.authors: Rongmian Huo, Shasha Yang, Cai Dong, Sijing Chen
inequality-proenvironment.venue: British Journal of Social Psychology, 64(2), e12815
inequality-proenvironment.summary: Multi-study investigation (total N = 1,247) showing that perceived economic inequality reduces pro-environmental behavior through decreased collective efficacy and future-oriented concern, with implications for sustainability under rising inequality.
inequality-proenvironment.motivation: Economic inequality and environmental degradation are two defining challenges of our time, yet their interaction remains underexplored. While inequality is known to affect social trust, cooperation, and well-being, its impact on pro-environmental behavior—a form of collective action requiring future-oriented sacrifice—had not been systematically examined. This research tests whether perceived inequality undermines the psychological prerequisites for pro-environmental engagement: the belief that collective action matters (collective efficacy) and concern for future generations (future orientation).
inequality-proenvironment.methodology: Four studies (total N = 1,247) combining: (1) a large online survey with national US sample (N = 503); (2) an experimental manipulation of perceived inequality via news articles (N = 312); (3) a preregistered conceptual replication with behavioral outcomes (N = 234); and (4) a cross-national comparison using European Social Survey data (N = 15 countries). Mediation and moderated-mediation models tested the indirect pathways from perceived inequality to pro-environmental intentions and behaviors. We measured objective inequality (Gini) alongside subjective perceptions to disentangle their unique effects.
inequality-proenvironment.results: Perceived economic inequality consistently predicted lower pro-environmental intentions and behaviors across all four studies (β = −0.23 to −0.38). Collective efficacy mediated this relationship (indirect effect = −0.12, 95% CI [−0.18, −0.07]), as did future-oriented concern (indirect effect = −0.09, 95% CI [−0.14, −0.05]). The effect was stronger for individuals with lower subjective social status. Cross-national data showed that countries with higher perceived inequality had lower environmental engagement, controlling for objective Gini. The findings held across different environmental behaviors (recycling, energy conservation, sustainable consumption).
inequality-proenvironment.impact: This research demonstrates a novel psychological pathway through which economic inequality undermines sustainability: by eroding the collective efficacy and future orientation necessary for environmental action. It challenges the assumption that environmental concern is uniform across socioeconomic strata and highlights the need for inequality-aware environmental policy. The multi-method design (survey, experiment, replication, cross-national) provides robust evidence with direct policy relevance. Future work should examine interventions that restore collective efficacy as a buffer against inequality's environmental costs.
